scenes.title: Cold open
scenes.draft: A cold case begins with paperwork, not drama: a call, a report, a box of evidence on a shelf. We follow a clearly labelled composite case, not a real one, to show how a case goes cold and how it is reopened. A woman is reported missing by her sister, then found dead. Detectives collect evidence, interview family and co-workers, and build a timeline. Nothing is enough to charge anyone. Within years the lead detective retires and the case is paused rather than closed. There is no single national definition of a cold case. We will walk through the second investigation, step by step, and mark what is confirmed, disputed and unknown.
on_screen_text: Composite case: not a real case, no real people

scenes.title: The timeline, sourced
scenes.draft: Every review starts with the old file, read slowly from page one: reports, interviews, photographs, evidence logs, lab results and tips. The investigator rebuilds a timeline in which every event is tied to a source and conflicts are recorded, not resolved by guesswork. NIJ's July 2019 best-practices guide sets out twenty-three recommendations in five areas and stresses modernizing the case file and confirming evidence still exists. A second timeline matters too: the tools. CODIS began as a pilot in 1990, the DNA Identification Act followed in 1994, and the national index went live in 1998. Newer DNA methods can now work with old or degraded samples. The gap between the two timelines is where the second investigation begins.

scenes.title: Bodycam: the response
scenes.draft: Body and dash cameras can record a scene before anyone has a theory, which makes them valuable years later. Our composite case predates wide body-camera use, so its record is reports and photographs. Whether footage can be shown publicly depends on state law and agency policy; there is no single national rule, and BJA's toolkit covers release policy. This channel uses only official releases, never leaked, sealed, juvenile or re-uploaded footage, keeps agency redactions, and adds its own blur. No real bodycam is used in this video. The first response also fixes the chain of custody: the evidence log shows three items were never tested.
on_screen_text: Release rules vary by state and agency
Evidence log: 3 items never sent to the lab

scenes.title: What the investigation found
scenes.draft: NIJ recommends separate cold case units with experienced investigators assigned full time and access to a lab. The team selects cases with testable evidence and living witnesses. In our composite case, retesting fingernail scrapings produces a male profile. It is searched locally, then at state and national CODIS levels; matches are confirmed before they become leads, and hits can arrive years later. The search finds nothing. Forensic genetic genealogy looks for relatives instead. The DOJ's 2019 interim policy, effective November 1, reserves it for violent crimes and unidentified remains, expects a CODIS search first, and limits arrests based on genetic association. A family tree yields a name; a direct DNA comparison then matches.
on_screen_text: A genealogy result is a lead, not an identification

scenes.title: Court and official record
scenes.draft: A match is where the legal process begins. A prosecutor decides whether to charge, weighing everything beyond DNA. Charging creates a public record: a sworn probable cause affidavit, a charging document, a docket. The court record is the strongest research source, ahead of news and far ahead of videos like this one. Under the FBI's UCR program, a case is cleared by arrest when someone is arrested, charged and turned over for prosecution, which is not a conviction. Exceptional clearances cover cases where an arrest is impossible, such as the offender's death. Our composite suspect is charged and presumed innocent.

scenes.title: What remains disputed / unknown
scenes.draft: Genetic genealogy is established but disputed: it can identify people who never took a test through their relatives, and users may not have expected police matching. Supporters point to solved violent crimes. Rules differ by place; Maryland and Montana regulated early, and Maryland and Washington DC prohibit familial searching of their databases. There is no single national count of cold cases, so that number is marked unknown. Clearance is not conviction. Pressure to close a case can create early certainty, so good practice re-examines evidence and shares the full file with the defense. Some questions may never be answered.
on_screen_text: Unknown: national number of cold cases

scenes.title: Aftermath and closing
scenes.draft: For families, the end of an investigation is a phone call or a knock on the door. NIJ's guide covers victim-centered, trauma-informed contact, careful media handling, and sustaining units beyond short grants. Retelling the composite case: careful original packaging and records made it possible for a later team, with better tools, to find an answer. Cold cases are usually solved by records kept and evidence preserved, not by one brilliant insight. The channel's promise is to tell real stories the same way: slowly, with sources, and with care, marking what is confirmed, disputed and unknown.
